results.summary: This design subtracts two 4-bit binary numbers using 2's complement subtraction, implemented with four full adders built from XOR and AND gates. The two 4-bit operands are applied to the eight input pins, and the 8-bit result drives the segments of a seven-segment display. Testing is done by entering two 4-bit binary numbers on the inputs and observing the displayed difference. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the output encoding or how negative results are shown.

This project implements a full adder using two 4:1 multiplexers instead of conventional gates, with the sum and carry outputs driving a seven-segment display. Three inputs A, B and Cin are provided on input pins, and the design is clocked at 1 Hz. Testing involves setting the clock and applying two 3-bit binary numbers, then reading the sum and carry on the display. The documentation is somewhat inconsistent about the number of inputs and the role of the clock.

This design uses two input bits to sequentially display the letters H, O, L and A on a seven-segment display. The four combinations 00, 01, 10 and 11 select which letter is shown. The project is described in Spanish and appears to be a simple demonstration or test chip. The documentation is very thin and does not explain the internal logic or the exact mapping of inputs to letters.

This is a four-state Moore finite state machine intended for a microrobot that detects water contamination, with two sensor inputs and two motor enable outputs. The state transitions are defined by a truth table, and the current state is stored in D flip-flops. The design requires external hardware including a 3-electrode sensor and motors, and some state bits are also routed to seven-segment display segments. The documentation is clear and includes a complete truth table, though the display outputs are not fully explained.

This design monitors a water tank level using two inputs and drives four LEDs to indicate Full, Half1, Half2 and Empty states, plus a motor control output. It uses D flip-flops for synchronization and state storage, and the motor starts when the tank is empty and stops when full. Testing involves a clock and two inputs, with five outputs connected to LEDs and a motor indicator. The documentation is somewhat unclear about the exact input encoding and the role of the clock.

This project implements a 5-to-1 multiplexer that selects one of five inputs based on three select lines and displays the selected input on a seven-segment display. The select lines are labeled S1, S2 and S3, with S3 also connected to the clock pin. Testing involves applying different select combinations such as 000 for I1, 100 for I2, 001 for I3, 101 for I4 and 111 for I5. The documentation is brief and the select encoding is not fully consistent with a standard 5-to-1 mux.

This is a two-minute toothbrush timer that divides a 10 kHz clock to produce 30-second increments, with each increment indicated by a segment on the seven-segment display. Each of the four increments can be gated by an enable switch so the user must acknowledge completion before moving on, and at the end all middle segments flash. A pause input freezes the timer, and a reset input restarts it. The documentation is detailed and includes testing instructions, though it notes that the first increment may be shorter than 30 seconds after a hard reset.

This design implements a 3-bit wide, 4-position register file using multiplexers for address decoding and data storage. It provides separate write and read addresses, a write enable, and outputs for the read data plus internal state and an inverted write enable. Testing involves setting the data bits and write address with write enable toggled to store a value, then setting the read address to retrieve it. The documentation is concise but sufficient to understand the basic operation.

This is a customized UART string transmitter that sends the fixed string "EDM!" using five 21-bit shift registers, with a 300 Hz clock and a 300 baud rate. It is a copy of a previous Tiny Tapeout design and requires an external MCU or UART-to-USB adapter connected to the TX output pin. Testing involves setting the clock, load and output enable switches appropriately and receiving the string on a serial terminal. The documentation is brief but includes clear testing steps and acknowledges the design's origin.

This is a Simon Says memory game where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors, each associated with a tone. The sequence is shown on four LEDs and played through a speaker, and the user responds using four buttons. The game supports four clock speeds selected by two inputs, and it plays level-up and game-over sounds. It requires external hardware including four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, and optionally a speaker or buzzer.
